qs.q: A patient presenting with posterior cervical lymphadenopathy and intermittent fever after a tsetse fly bite is found to have a trypanosomal chancre. What is this classic lymph node sign called?
qs.e: Winterbottom’s sign refers to posterior cervical lymphadenopathy seen in the hemolymphatic stage of African trypanosomiasis. Romana's sign is associated with Chagas disease.

qs.q: Researchers are setting up traps in a known focus of West African sleeping sickness. Which tsetse fly species is the primary vector for Trypanosoma brucei gambiense?
qs.e: Glossina palpalis and G. tachinoides transmit West African sleeping sickness caused by T. b. gambiense. Glossina morsitans transmits the East African form.

ai.subject: Microbiology & immunology
ai.summary: The tsetse fly (Glossina) transmits African trypanosomiasis (sleeping sickness) by injecting metacyclic trypomastigotes during a bite. The disease progresses from a haemolymphatic stage to a meningo‑encephalitic stage, causing fever, neurological signs and death if untreated.

sections.p: Glossina species are hematophagous flies endemic to sub‑Saharan Africa. They are the sole biological vectors of Trypanosoma brucei subspecies that cause human African trypanosomiasis (HAT).
b: Found in riverine and savanna habitats
Female flies live 1–3 months, feeding every 2–3 days
Control relies on traps, insecticide‑treated targets, and sterile‑male release

sections.p: Trypanosoma brucei is a flagellated protozoan that exists as bloodstream‑form trypomastigotes and tissue‑stage ‘stumpy’ forms. It evades immunity by antigenic variation of its variant surface glycoprotein (VSG).
b: Two human‑infective subspecies: T. b. gambiense (chronic) and T. b. rhodesiense (acute)
VSG switching leads to waves of parasitaemia
Resistant to complement, survives in plasma

sections.p: During a blood meal, an infected tsetse injects metacyclic trypomastigotes into the host. Parasites multiply in the blood, then cross the blood‑brain barrier in the second stage.
b: Rarely via transfusion or congenital transmission

sections.p: Human African trypanosomiasis presents in two stages. Stage 1 (haemolymphatic) features fever, lymphadenopathy, and chancre. Stage 2 (meningo‑encephalitic) adds sleep disturbance, psychiatric changes, and coma.
b: Stage 1: fever, headache, arthralgia, enlarged posterior cervical nodes
Stage 2: daytime somnolence, night‑time insomnia, personality change, gait disturbance

sections.p: Confirmatory diagnosis requires detection of parasites in blood, lymph, or CSF, and staging by CSF analysis.
b: If microscopy unavailable, treat presumptively in high‑risk settings after serology
PCR is sensitive but rarely accessible in low‑resource areas

t.a: Microscopy of blood/lymph (wet mount, concentration techniques)
t.b: Detects active infection; a positive slide confirms HAT regardless of stage
Determines stage: >5 WBC/µL or presence of parasites indicates stage 2

t.a: Serologic rapid test (CATT) for T. b. gambiense
t.b: Screening tool; positive result prompts parasitological confirmation

sections.p: Therapy is stage‑specific: drugs that cross the blood‑brain barrier are required for stage 2. Vector control reduces incidence.
b: Stage 1: pentamidine (T. b. gambiense) or suramin (T. b. rhodesiense) – chosen for poor CNS penetration
Stage 2: eflornithine (T. b. gambiense) or nifurtimox‑eflornithine combination; melarsoprol for melarsoprol‑sensitive cases – selected for CNS activity
Avoid melarsoprol when possible due to severe encephalopathic toxicity

sections.p: Key points to remember for exams:
b: Two subspecies differ in epidemiology: gambiense (West‑Central Africa, chronic) vs rhodesiense (East Africa, acute)
Stage 2 diagnosis hinges on CSF WBC >5/µL or parasites in CSF
Pentamidine treats stage 1 gambiense; melarsoprol is last‑line for stage 2 when other drugs unavailable

whenToSeekHelp: High fever with chancre after a tsetse bite
Progressive sleep disturbance, confusion, or gait instability
Any neurologic decline in a patient from endemic area

faq.q: Can sleeping sickness be transmitted by other insects?
faq.a: No, only Glossina species are proven biological vectors; other flies may mechanically transmit but not sustain the parasite.

faq.q: Why is melarsoprol rarely used today?
faq.a: It causes severe post‑treatment encephalopathy in up to 10 % of patients and has high mortality, so safer drugs are preferred.

faq.q: Is there a vaccine for African trypanosomiasis?
faq.a: No, antigenic variation of VSG prevents effective vaccine development.
